extracted.intended_audience: sketch comedy writers / aspiring SNL writers and late-night TV writers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidance for constructing short televised sketch comedy (especially for SNL): establishing a clear premise quickly, structuring three rounds of escalation, ending with a button, and writing to the cast/audience. Emphasizes what survives read-throughs and what to avoid (local jokes, non-performable material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold open premise stated in first 30 seconds
rubrics_metrics.description: Cold open premise: stated in first 30 seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sketch's premise should be clear and audible very quickly — within the first 30 seconds — so the audience immediately knows what the joke-world is about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise lock by 60 seconds
rubrics_metrics.description: Premise lock: by 60 seconds, the audience knows the rules of this world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By the one-minute mark the sketch must have 'locked' its world: what is allowed, what's at stake, and the internal logic so that escalations make sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightening — Round 1 (clear escalation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heightening Round 1: a clear escalation of the premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first escalation should clearly raise the stakes or deepen the joke — not merely repeat the initial premise but move it forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightening — Round 2 (complication/new angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heightening Round 2: a complication / new angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second round introduces a complication or a fresh perspective that changes the audience's expectations and further escalates the comedic premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightening — Round 3 (absurdist version)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The third escalation pushes the premise to its most extreme or absurd conclusion — the payoff of the pattern established earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Button (final beat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Button: a final beat that buttons the sketch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End with a definitive final beat that ties the sketch off (a 'button') — the last laugh or image that completes the premise and leaves the audience with a clear ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightening must escalate, not repeat
rubrics_metrics.description: The sketch is dead if any round just REPEATS rather than HEIGHTENS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid redundancy: each round must add something new. Repeating the same joke/beat without escalation kills momentum and makes the sketch feel flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast members have tonal ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Each cast member has a tonal range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the performers' strengths and typical tones — write parts that sit inside their believable/employable range rather than imposing unfamiliar tones on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the lead something to DO
rubrics_metrics.description: A sketch must give the lead something they can DO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads should have an active role (a physical action, a clear objective, reactions) — not just deliver jokes; giving someone something to do creates stronger, performable comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't write sketches the cast can't perform
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing a sketch the cast can't perform = written for yourself, not for the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the material relies on skills or tonalities your cast can't credibly deliver, it's not ready for the show. Tailor material to the ensemble or rewrite to fit performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wednesday read-through volume and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: 40+ sketches read for the show; ~12 chosen for blocking; ~8 make air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the production funnel — many sketches are read; only a few get staged and fewer still air. This shapes expectations for what to submit and how to test jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jokes must survive a flat read
rubrics_metrics.description: The Wednesday read teaches you which jokes survive a flat read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches must read well aloud with minimal staging; if jokes fall flat in a table read, they likely won't survive rehearsal or TV. Write and test for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise test — can it be stated in one sentence?
rubrics_metrics.description: Can the premise be stated in one sentence?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can't boil the idea down to a single-sentence premise, the sketch may be unfocused or overcomplicated — clarity of premise predicts stronger sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise test — internal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the world of the sketch internally consistent?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sketch's rules and logic must hold across beats so escalations feel earned; contradictions weaken the audience's suspension of disbelief and the comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise test — generates at least three escalations
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the premise generate at least three escalations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong premise should naturally yield multiple distinct escalations (rounds) so the structure (setup → escalation → escalation → absurd payoff) feels organic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise test — has a button
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the premise have a button?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure there's a satisfying final beat or image that can serve as the sketch's button; if the premise lacks one, the sketch can fizzle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the local-joke trap
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'local joke' is a joke that works for the writers' room but not the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut or rewrite industry-insider jokes, obscure references, and political-insider language. Aim for jokes the national TV audience will get; specificity is good, but not obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drezen-inflected working rubric (summary checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drezen-Inflected Working Rubric: 1) Premise stated in 30 seconds? 2) World locked by 60 seconds? 3) Three rounds of heightening (not repeating)? 4) Button at the end? 5) Cast member has something to DO? 6) No local jokes the country won't get?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this concise checklist as a quick pass/fail filter during drafting and rewriting. It restates the core craft rules in a compact, actionable form.
